outcome.question: EDC coupling in DCM gave me 34%, but our own solvent screen said a chlorinated solvent should sit around 70. What did we get wrong?
outcome.answer:
I'll help you dig into the discrepancy. Let me gather what your screening work found and trace what might have happened.Found it. Let me get the full details from both notes:**The answer: temperature ramp, not solvent choice.**

Your failure note documents exactly this issue [[failure-dcm-amide-coupling]]: DCM at 34% was run at **20 °C throughout**, but the solvent screen that predicted ~70% used a **0 °C start** with an implied temperature ramp. That difference is load-bearing for EDC couplings.

The mechanism is straightforward: EDC activates the carboxylic acid to an O-acylisourea intermediate, which is reactive but also susceptible to rearrangement at warmer temperatures. Keeping the initial activation step cold (0 °C) slows the rearrangement pathway and gives the amine nucleophile time to intercept it before it degrades to the urea byproduct. At 20 °C from the start, rearrangement wins and you see the yield floor.

**What the screening actually told you**: your solvent screen ([[opt-amide-solvent]]) ranked DCM at 12 points below DMF/MeCN (which hit 79–81%) and found 2-MeTHF at 76%. That ranking is real *at the conditions the screen used* — but it assumed proper temperature control. The implication is that **DCM belongs in that 70–80% band when you use the right temperature protocol**, not that it is intrinsically 34%.

The distilled playbook [[playbook-amide-coupling-additive]] is what holds here: the chemistry (the activation and nucleophilic attack pathway) does not change with solvent choice, so the temperature ramp is the lever, and DCM—which is apolar and a good solvent for both the activated carboxylic acid and the amine — should behave like the screen predicted once you run it cold.

**What to do next**: repeat the DCM run at 0 °C start (and the ramp your screen used) to verify you get back to the ~70% level. If you do, the takeaway is "temperature control is critical for EDC on this substrate," not "DCM is bad." If you do not, there may be a second factor — additive, catalyst loading, stoichiometry — that differed between the screen and your recent run.
